title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

deep.reconstruction: Problem: use the observed middle of a lunar eclipse to fix the Moon's true longitude in its orbit. This is the classical method of using eclipses to calibrate lunar tables. The earlier sections give the setup. U is the longitude of the shadow centre (Sun + 180°) at mid-eclipse and L the Moon's longitude in its orbit at that instant. m and n are the hourly motions of Sun and Moon in arc-seconds, and k is the hourly regression of the node. x is the argument of latitude (shadow longitude minus node longitude), ρ is the inclination, and g = π/648000 converts seconds to radians. The previous page found that the instant at which orbital longitude equals shadow longitude falls τ = (m+n+2k) sin2x tan²(ρ/2) / (g(n−m)²) hours after mid-eclipse. At that instant U + mτ = L + nτ. Hence L = U − (n−m)τ = U − (m+n+2k) sin2x tan²(ρ/2) / (g(n−m)) arc-seconds, which is the formula opening this page. §12 is the recipe: take the true solar longitude, add or subtract 6 signs to get U, then subtract this quantity to get the Moon's orbital longitude at mid-eclipse. Euler argues that an error of a few minutes in the node longitude (hence in x) is negligible, because the correction is itself only a few minutes. §13 says the inclination from existing tables is accurate enough. He factors the correction as (1/g) sin2x tan²(ρ/2) times (m+n+2k)/(n−m) = 1 + 2(m+k)/(n−m), and tabulates the first factor for x = 0°–10°. The table uses symmetric arguments (VI signs; V and XI signs with complementary degrees) and lists the inclination at each argument (5°17'1" falling to 5°16'29"), i.e. a variable inclination is built into the table. Check: with ρ = 5°17'1", tan²(ρ/2)/g ≈ 439.2", so the 2° entry is 439.2 × sin4° ≈ 30.6" ✓. With ρ = 5°16'29", tan²(ρ/2)/g ≈ 437.7", so the 10° entry is 437.7 × sin20° ≈ 149.7" = 2'29.7" ✓. The footnote and margin add the reduction to the ecliptic. The ecliptic longitude is the orbital longitude minus (1/g) sin2x tan²(ρ/2), so the total multiplier becomes (m+n+2k)/(n−m) + 1 = (2n+2k)/(n−m). The margin evaluates this with m = 148", k = 8" (the node's hourly regression, ≈19.3°/yr) and n = 2023" − 258" cos v (lunar hourly motion with anomaly v). For cos v = 0 this gives 4062/1875 ≈ 2 1/6, the multiplier quoted in the margin.
errors: Marginal note: for cos v = 1 the multiplier (2n+2k)/(n−m) should be 3546/1617, not 3546/1875. For cos v = −1 it should be 4578/2133, not 4578/1875. The denominator n−m was not updated when n changed; only the numerators are right. It is unclear whether the slip is Euler's or the editor's.

Marginal wording: 2 1/6 ≈ 4062/1875 is the mean value of the ecliptic multiplier (2n+2k)/(n−m). The orbital multiplier 1 + 2(m+k)/(n−m) is about 1 1/6. The margin's text uses 'in ecliptica' for both multipliers, which is loose.

The formula drops the higher-order tan⁴(ρ/2) term, as stated on the previous page. The equation-of-the-orbit terms depending on the angle η are neglected, which is justified on the next page. These are approximations, not errors.

ideas.what: Determining the Moon's true orbital longitude from the middle of a lunar eclipse, corrected for the inclination of the orbit and for the Sun's and node's motion.
ideas.modern_name: Eclipse-based calibration of lunar longitude (opposition reduction)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ancient practice (Hipparchus, Ptolemy); 18th-century refinements by Euler, T. Mayer and others
ideas.where_published: Euler's lunar theory works (E187 Theoria motus lunae 1753, E418 1772) treat lunar tables; this specific chapter is from the posthumous 1862 publication

ideas.what: Reduction to the ecliptic: ecliptic longitude = orbital longitude − tan²(ρ/2) sin 2x to first order.
ideas.where_published: Standard in Euler's lunar tables and in astronomical textbooks of the period

ideas.what: A table of (1/g) sin2x tan²(ρ/2) with the inclination varying with the argument, to be scaled by a factor computed from the hourly motions.

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine practical spherical astronomy for reducing eclipse observations. The formulas and tables are correct apart from a slip in the marginal denominators. Nothing here appears new or uncredited.
transcription_corrections: Marginal fractions: the printed denominators are all 1875; the correct values for cos v = ±1 would be 1617 and 2133 respectively (a note on the content, not a misreading).
'angulus inclinationis ☊ = ρ' is printed as such; the ☊ sign stands loosely for the inclination of the nodal orbit.
The table header reads '○ Sign. VI Sign. Subtrahe.' at the top and 'Adde: V sign. XI sign.' at the bottom with complementary degrees 30–20 — confirmed against the image.
